name: The Loch Ness Monster
description: A long-necked something said to live in the deep, dark water of Loch Ness

debut.title: Highland water-beast lore and the Inverness Courier's 1933 report

legend: Loch Ness is 23 miles long and more than 200 metres deep, and its peat-dark water hides whatever is in it. The oldest tale is in Adomnán's Life of St Columba, written around the year 700, in which the saint orders a 'water beast' back into the River Ness in 565. The modern monster was born in 1933, after a new road along the north shore opened up the view: on 2 May the Inverness Courier reported that Aldie Mackay had seen something large rolling and plunging in the loch, and that summer George Spicer described a creature crossing the road in front of his car. The Daily Mail hired big-game hunter Marmaduke Wetherell, whose 'footprints' turned out to have been made with a dried hippopotamus foot. On 21 April 1934 the paper printed the famous 'Surgeon's Photograph', credited to London doctor Robert Kenneth Wilson; in 1994 it was revealed that Wetherell's stepson Christian Spurling had built the head and neck onto a toy submarine. Sonar sweeps such as Operation Deepscan (1987) and a 2018 environmental DNA survey found no reptile, but a great deal of eel. Folklorists note that Highland lochs had water-horses, or kelpies, long before anyone had a camera.

myths.explanation: In 1994 it emerged that Christian Spurling had modelled the head and neck on a toy submarine for his stepfather, Marmaduke Wetherell, who wanted revenge on the Daily Mail.

myths.claim: The first written account of a Ness monster is from the 6th century.
myths.explanation: Adomnán's Life of St Columba, written around 700, describes the saint banishing a water beast in the River Ness in 565, though in the river rather than the loch.
Plesiosaurs died out 66 million years ago, and Loch Ness was solid ice until about 10,000 years ago. A cold freshwater loch could not feed a breeding population either.

myths.claim: A DNA survey of the loch found a great deal of eel.
myths.explanation: The 2018 environmental DNA study found no reptile DNA at all, but eels everywhere. A very large eel remains the scientists' favourite candidate.

myths.claim: Loch Ness holds more water than every lake in England and Wales put together.
myths.explanation: It is so long and deep that it contains more fresh water than all the lakes of England and Wales combined.

quotes.text: Thou shalt go no further, nor touch the man; go back with all speed.
quotes.speaker: St Columba, to the water beast
quotes.source: Adomnán, Life of St Columba (c. 700), Book II, in Wentworth Huyshe's 1905 translation

powers: Hiding in 200 metres of peat-dark water
Appearing only when the camera is out of focus
A neck that rises and dips without warning
Turning a quiet Highland loch into a tourist magnet
legacy: The Secret of the Loch (1934), the first Nessie film
The Loch Ness Investigation Bureau, which watched the water from 1962 to 1972
The Loch Ness Centre at Drumnadrochit

hostIntro: Tonight's guest has been photographed hundreds of times and never once in focus. She's Scottish, she's shy, and she's quite possibly an eel.
